overview: Sinosauropteryx prima was the first non-avian dinosaur found with direct evidence of feathers — described from the Yixian Formation of Liaoning, China in 1996. Its simple, unbranched filamentous integument (proto-feathers) covers the head, back and tail and represents the simplest feather-like structure known: hollow, hair-like filaments without barbules or barbs.

The original description of Sinosauropteryx triggered immediate scientific controversy: critics argued the filaments were decayed collagen fibres, not feathers. Subsequent analyses of feather microstructure, including melanosome analysis revealing an orange-and-white ringed tail, have comprehensively confirmed the feather interpretation and established Sinosauropteryx as a cornerstone of feathered dinosaur research.

fossilSites.name: Yixian Formation
fossilSites.note: Lower Cretaceous lacustrine deposits with exceptional soft-tissue preservation; the locus of most feathered non-avian dinosaur discoveries.

articles.title: Discovery and the feather controversy
articles.body: The first specimen reached Ji Qiang of the National Geological Museum of China in 1996; he and colleagues described it that year. Philip Currie and Chen Pei-ji independently confirmed the filamentous integument. The controversy over whether the structures were feathers or collagen fibres persisted for a decade until chemical and structural analyses — showing melanosomes, hollow structures and consistent diameter distributions — confirmed their feather nature.

articles.title: Colour reconstruction
articles.body: Sinosauropteryx is the first dinosaur to have its colour pattern reconstructed with chemical evidence. Analysis of melanosomes (melanin granelles) in the tail filaments reveals two different melanosome types alternating along the tail: phaeomelanosomes (rusty orange) and eumelanosomes (dark). This creates a vivid orange-and-white striped tail, probably used for display, analogous to ringed tails in modern mammals.

articles.title: Stomach contents
articles.body: Several specimens preserve stomach contents. One contains a small mammal (a shrew-like tribosphenidan), another a small lizard. This shows Sinosauropteryx was an active, opportunistic predator of small vertebrates. A third specimen appears to contain eggs, possibly indicating female reproductive anatomy rather than stomach content.

fossilRecord.material: Several complete or near-complete specimens with feather impressions and stomach contents.
fossilRecord.completeness: Exceptional — feathers and diet directly preserved
fossilRecord.paleo: Early Cretaceous lake and forest ecosystem of northeastern China.
fossilRecord.evidence: Filamentous feather impressions and melanosome analysis allowed colour reconstruction; stomach contents preserve lizard and mammal prey.

record.description: Sinosauropteryx was a small compsognathid-like coelurosaur from the Yixian Formation, known from multiple articulated skeletons with filamentous integument and some gut contents.
facts: It provided the first widely accepted non-avian dinosaur integument outside birds.
Melanosome studies support a banded tail and reddish-brown pattern in at least one specimen, not a universal genus-wide palette.
Recent analyses disagree over the monophyly and family-level name of compsognathid-like theropods.

review.ageReviewNote: High-precision dating brackets the Yixian Formation at 125.755-124.122 Ma, within the Barremian on the current time scale.

residualUncertainty: Colour and diet observations are specimen-specific.

evidence.material: Multiple articulated skeletons with filamentous integument, pigmentation and some gut contents.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Do not generalise one specimen's colour or stomach contents to all individuals, or present one family assignment as settled.
